[Amazon](/wiki/Amazon_(company) "Amazon (company)"), the world's largest company by revenue since 2026[[1]](#cite_note-1)

This list comprises the world's largest companies by [consolidated](/wiki/Consolidation_(business) "Consolidation (business)") [revenue](/wiki/Revenue "Revenue"), according to the annual [*Fortune* Global 500](/wiki/Fortune_Global_500 "Fortune Global 500") rankings and other sources.[[2]](#cite_note-2) Among the 50 largest companies, 23 are in the [United States](/wiki/United_States "United States"), 17 are in [Asia](/wiki/Asia "Asia"), and 10 are in [Europe](/wiki/Europe "Europe").[[3]](#cite_note-3)

This list is limited to the largest 50 companies, all of which reported annual revenues exceeding US$130 billion. This list is incomplete, as not all companies disclose their information to the media or general public.[[4]](#cite_note-4) Data reflects the most recent [fiscal year](/wiki/Fiscal_year "Fiscal year"), primarily 2024 or 2025.

From 1903 to 1952, the major leagues consisted of two eight-team leagues[[a]](#cite_note-68) whose 16 teams were located in ten cities, all in the northeastern and mid-western United States: New York City had three teams and [Boston](/wiki/Boston "Boston"), Chicago, [Philadelphia](/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia"), and [St. Louis](/wiki/St._Louis "St. Louis") each had two teams. St. Louis was the southernmost and westernmost city with a major league team. The longest possible road trip, from Boston to St. Louis, took about 24 hours by railroad. After a half-century of stability, starting in the 1950s, teams began to move out of cities with multiple teams into cities that had not had them before. From 1953 to 1955, three teams moved to new cities: the [Boston Braves](/wiki/Boston_Braves "Boston Braves") became the [Milwaukee Braves](/wiki/Milwaukee_Braves "Milwaukee Braves"), the [St. Louis Browns](/wiki/St._Louis_Browns "St. Louis Browns") became the [Baltimore Orioles](/wiki/Baltimore_Orioles "Baltimore Orioles"), and the [Philadelphia Athletics](/wiki/Philadelphia_Athletics "Philadelphia Athletics") became the [Kansas City Athletics](/wiki/Kansas_City_Athletics "Kansas City Athletics").

They also talked about the moment when the group started their musical endeavor and their realizations of pursuing individual careers after working together for several years. [![refer to caption](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/33/Oil_Balance.png/500px-Oil_Balance.png)](/wiki/File:Oil_Balance.png)

Countries by net oil exports, 2008

The differing economic needs of OPEC member states often affect the internal debates behind OPEC production quotas. Poorer members have pushed for production cuts from fellow members, to increase the price of oil and thus their own revenues.[[117]](#cite_note-owen032010-117) These proposals conflict with Saudi Arabia's stated long-term strategy of being a partner with the world's economic powers to ensure a steady flow of oil that would support economic expansion.[[118]](#cite_note-118)

Part of the basis for this policy is the Saudi concern that overly expensive oil or unreliable supply will drive industrial nations to conserve energy and develop alternative fuels, curtailing the worldwide demand for oil and eventually leaving unneeded barrels in the ground.[[119]](#cite_note-119) To this point, Saudi Oil Minister Yamani famously remarked in 1973: "The Stone Age didn't end because we ran out of stones."[[120]](#cite_note-120)

To elucidate Saudi Arabia's contemporary approach, in 2024, Saudi Energy Minister Prince [Abdulaziz bin Salman](/wiki/Abdulaziz_bin_Salman "Abdulaziz bin Salman") articulated a stance that reflects how the kingdom has adapted to the evolving economic needs within OPEC and the broader international community. Emphasizing the need for a balanced and fair global [energy transition](/wiki/Energy_transition "Energy transition"), he highlighted the importance of diversifying energy sources and noted significant investments in [natural gas](/wiki/Natural_gas "Natural gas"), [petrochemicals](/wiki/Petrochemical "Petrochemical"), and [renewables](/wiki/Renewable_energy "Renewable energy"). Main article: [Rain shadow](/wiki/Rain_shadow "Rain shadow")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e2/Wa_rain_map.JPG/250px-Wa_rain_map.JPG)](/wiki/File:Wa_rain_map.JPG)

Washington experiences extensive variation in rainfall.

Rainfall in Washington varies dramatically going from east to west. The Olympic Peninsula's western side receives as much as 160 inches (4,100 mm) of precipitation annually, making it the wettest area of the 48 conterminous states and a [temperate rainforest](/wiki/Temperate_rainforest "Temperate rainforest"). Weeks may pass without a clear day. The western slopes of the Cascade Range receive some of the heaviest annual snowfall (in some places more than 200 inches or 5,100 millimeters water equivalent) in the country. In the rain shadow area east of the Cascades, the annual precipitation is only 6 inches (150 mm). Precipitation then increases again eastward toward the Rocky Mountains (about 120 miles (190 km) east of the Idaho border).

The Olympic mountains and Cascades compound this climatic pattern by causing [orographic lift](/wiki/Orographic_lift "Orographic lift") of the air masses blown inland from the Pacific Ocean, resulting in the windward side of the mountains receiving high levels of precipitation and the leeward side receiving low levels. This occurs most dramatically around the Olympic Mountains and the Cascade Range. In both cases, the windward slopes facing southwest receive high precipitation and mild, cool temperatures. While the Puget Sound lowlands are known for clouds and rain in the winter, the western slopes of the Cascades receive larger amounts of precipitation, often falling as snow at higher elevations.[[89]](#cite_note-90) [Mount Baker](/wiki/Mount_Baker "Mount Baker"), near the state's northern border, is one of the snowiest places in the world. The [Philadelphia Quakers](/wiki/Philadelphia_Quakers_(NHL) "Philadelphia Quakers (NHL)"), who played during the [1930–31 season](/wiki/1930%E2%80%9331_NHL_season "1930–31 NHL season"), was Philadelphia's first [NHL](/wiki/National_Hockey_League "National Hockey League") franchise.

Prior to 1967, Philadelphia had only iced a team in the NHL in the [1930–31 season](/wiki/1930%E2%80%9331_NHL_season "1930–31 NHL season"), when the financially struggling [Pittsburgh Pirates](/wiki/Pittsburgh_Pirates_(NHL) "Pittsburgh Pirates (NHL)") relocated in 1930 as the [Philadelphia Quakers](/wiki/Philadelphia_Quakers_(NHL) "Philadelphia Quakers (NHL)"), playing at The Arena at 46th and Market Streets. The club, garbed in orange and black like today's Flyers, was coached by [J. Cooper Smeaton](/wiki/J._Cooper_Smeaton "J. Cooper Smeaton"), who was to be elected to the [Hockey Hall of Fame](/wiki/Hockey_Hall_of_Fame "Hockey Hall of Fame") 30 years later, for his far more notable role as an NHL referee. Among the young Quakers' skaters in 1930–31 was another future Hall of Famer in 19-year-old rookie center [Syd Howe](/wiki/Syd_Howe "Syd Howe"). The Quakers' only "claim to fame" was to establish a single season NHL record for futility which has stood ever since, by compiling a dismal record of 4–36–4, still the fewest games ever won in a season by an NHL club. The Quakers quietly suspended operations after that single dreadful campaign to again leave the Can-Am League's [Philadelphia Arrows](/wiki/Philadelphia_Arrows "Philadelphia Arrows") as Philadelphia's lone hockey team. The Quakers' dormant NHL franchise was finally canceled by the league in 1936.[[10]](#cite_note-12)[[11]](#cite_note-13)

The post-war years saw scholars renewing broken bonds through numerous conventions, expansion of the campus, and the introduction of distribution requirements.[[104]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeitch1978139-105)[[105]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOberdorfer1995137-106) The period saw the desegregation of Princeton, which was stimulated by changes to the New Jersey constitution.[[106]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBradley2010115-107) Princeton began undertaking a sharper focus towards research in the years after the war, with the construction of Firestone Library in 1948 and the establishment of the Forrestal Research Center in nearby [Plainsboro Township](/wiki/Plainsboro_Township,_New_Jersey "Plainsboro Township, New Jersey") in the 1950s.[[107]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOberdorfer1995158-108) Government sponsored research increased sharply, particularly in the physics and engineering departments,[[108]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOberdorfer1995165–166-109) with much of it occurring at the new Forrestal campus.[[109]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOberdorfer1995168-110) Though, as the years progressed, scientific research at the Forrestal campus declined, and in 1973, some of the land was converted to commercial and residential spaces.[[110]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOberdorfer1995170-111)

Between 1901 and 2017, the [Nobel Prizes](/wiki/Nobel_Prizes "Nobel Prizes") and the [Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences](/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences "Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences") were awarded 585 times to 923 people and organizations. With some receiving the Nobel Prize more than once, this makes a total of 892 individuals (including 844 men, 48 women) and 24 organizations.[[8]](#cite_note-8) Six Nobel laureates were not permitted by their governments to accept the Nobel Prize. [Adolf Hitler](/wiki/Adolf_Hitler "Adolf Hitler") forbade four Germans, [Richard Kuhn](/wiki/Richard_Kuhn "Richard Kuhn") (Chemistry, 1938), [Adolf Butenandt](/wiki/Adolf_Butenandt "Adolf Butenandt") (Chemistry, 1939), [Gerhard Domagk](/wiki/Gerhard_Domagk "Gerhard Domagk") (Physiology or Medicine, 1939) and [Carl von Ossietzky](/wiki/Carl_von_Ossietzky "Carl von Ossietzky") (Peace, 1936) from accepting their Nobel Prizes. The [Chinese government](/wiki/Government_of_China "Government of China") forbade [Liu Xiaobo](/wiki/Liu_Xiaobo "Liu Xiaobo") from accepting his Nobel Prize (Peace, 2010)[[9]](#cite_note-9) and the government of the [Soviet Union](/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") pressured [Boris Pasternak](/wiki/Boris_Pasternak "Boris Pasternak") (Literature, 1958) to decline his award. [Liu Xiaobo](/wiki/Liu_Xiaobo "Liu Xiaobo"), [Carl von Ossietzky](/wiki/Carl_von_Ossietzky "Carl von Ossietzky") and [Aung San Suu Kyi](/wiki/Aung_San_Suu_Kyi "Aung San Suu Kyi") were all awarded their Nobel Prize while in prison or detention.[[10]](#cite_note-10) Two Nobel laureates, [Jean-Paul Sartre](/wiki/Jean-Paul_Sartre "Jean-Paul Sartre") (Literature, 1964) and [Lê Ðức Thọ](/wiki/Le_Duc_Tho "Le Duc Tho") (Peace, 1973), declined the award; Sartre declined the award as he declined all official honors, and Thọ declined the award due to the situation Vietnam was in at the time.

**Miami**[[b]](#cite_note-12) is a [coastal](/wiki/East_Coast_of_the_United_States "East Coast of the United States") [city](/wiki/City "City") in the [U.S. state](/wiki/U.S._state "U.S. state") of [Florida](/wiki/Florida "Florida"). It is the [second-most populous city proper](/wiki/List_of_municipalities_in_Florida "List of municipalities in Florida") in Florida, with a population of 442,241 at the [2020 census](/wiki/2020_United_States_census "2020 United States census").[[5]](#cite_note-2020CensusPopulationByRace-6) The [Miami metropolitan area](/wiki/Miami_metropolitan_area "Miami metropolitan area") in [South Florida](/wiki/South_Florida "South Florida") has an estimated 6.39 million residents, ranking as the fifth-largest metropolitan area in the [Southeast](/wiki/Southeastern_United_States "Southeastern United States") and [eighth-largest metropolitan area](/wiki/Metropolitan_statistical_area#United_States "Metropolitan statistical area") in the United States.[[7]](#cite_note-2020Pop-8) Miami has the [third-largest skyline](/wiki/List_of_tallest_buildings_in_the_United_States#Cities_with_the_most_skyscrapers "List of tallest buildings in the United States") in the U.S. with over [300 high-rises](/wiki/List_of_tallest_buildings_in_Miami "List of tallest buildings in Miami"),[[11]](#cite_note-13) 70 of which exceed 491 ft (150 m).[[12]](#cite_note-14) It is the [county seat](/wiki/County_seat "County seat") of [Miami-Dade County](/wiki/Miami-Dade_County,_Florida "Miami-Dade County, Florida").
